title: Fertilise soil and attend to basic plant nutrition

lessons.title: Soil and how to prepare it
lessons.html:
What soil is made of

Soil is a mix of small rock pieces (sand, silt and clay), organic matter (rotten plants and dung), water, air and many small living things like earthworms.

Types of soil

SoilHow it feelsWhat it does
SandyRough, falls apart in your handDrains fast, dries out, loses fertiliser quickly
ClaySticky when wet, hard when dryHolds water and food, but can get waterlogged
LoamSoft and crumblyBest for most crops: holds water and drains well

Dark soil usually has more organic matter. Good soil is crumbly, smells earthy and has earthworms.

Preparing soil with hand tools

  • Spade or fork: dig and turn the soil.
  • Hoe: break clods and remove weeds.
  • Rake: level the soil and make a fine seedbed.
  • Wheelbarrow: carry compost and manure.

Low-technology ploughing

Some farms use a plough pulled by oxen or donkeys, or a small walk-behind tractor. Plough when the soil is moist, not too wet and not too dry. Plough across the slope, not up and down, to stop soil being washed away. This helps protect the soil, as the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 requires.

Safety

  • Wear boots and gloves.
  • Lift with your knees bent, not your back.
  • Keep tools sharp and carry them pointing down.
  • Keep away from the animals' hooves and the plough blade.

lessons.title: Plant food and signs of hunger
lessons.html:
What plants need

Plants need sunlight, water, air and food from the soil. The main foods (nutrients) are:

  • Nitrogen (N): for green leaves and growth.
  • Phosphorus (P): for roots, flowers and seeds.
  • Potassium (K): for strong plants, good fruit and resistance to disease.

Plants also need small amounts of other nutrients such as calcium, magnesium, sulphur, iron and zinc.

Signs that a plant is hungry

What you seePossible shortage
Old, bottom leaves turn pale yellow; plant grows slowlyNitrogen
Leaves dark green with purple or red colour, especially on young maizePhosphorus
Leaf edges turn yellow, then brown and dry, starting on old leavesPotassium
Yellow between the veins of old leaves; veins stay greenMagnesium
Yellow between the veins of young, new leavesIron
Tomato fruit with a black, dry patch at the bottom (blossom end rot)Calcium, often linked to uneven watering

Other problems such as too much water, too little water, disease or insects can look like hunger. Report what you see to your supervisor; a soil or leaf test can confirm the problem.

How to check plants in the field

  1. Walk through the land or garden slowly, along the rows.
  2. Look at old leaves and new leaves separately. Some shortages start on old leaves, others on new leaves.
  3. Compare sick plants with healthy plants next to them.
  4. Check the soil: is it very wet, very dry or hard?
  5. Write down the block or row number and what you saw.
  6. Tell your supervisor the same day. Do not add fertiliser on your own.

lessons.title: Applying fertiliser and making compost
lessons.html:
Fertiliser

Fertiliser is bought plant food. It comes in bags marked with three numbers, for example 2:3:2, which show the ratio of N, P and K. Your supervisor decides which fertiliser, how much and when. You apply it under close supervision.

How to apply fertiliser

  1. Wear gloves and a dust mask. Wash hands after.
  2. Use the measure your supervisor gives you, for example a cup or tin per plant or per metre of row.
  3. Put fertiliser in a band next to the row or in a ring around the plant, not touching the stem or seeds; it can burn them.
  4. Cover it lightly with soil.
  5. Water it in, or apply when the soil is moist.
  6. Do not spread fertiliser near rivers, dams or boreholes.

Never

  • Never use more than you are told. More fertiliser does not mean more crop; it burns plants and wastes money.
  • Never store fertiliser near food or water, and never eat or smoke while handling it.

Compost

Compost is rotten plant material and manure. It feeds the soil, helps sandy soil hold water and makes clay soil crumbly.

Making a compost heap

  1. Choose a shady spot near the garden.
  2. Layer dry material (dry grass, maize stalks, leaves), then green material (fresh weeds, vegetable peels), then manure, then a little soil.
  3. Repeat the layers until the heap is about waist high.
  4. Keep it damp like a squeezed sponge.
  5. Turn the heap every few weeks.
  6. It is ready when it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil.

Dig compost into the soil before planting, or put it around plants as mulch.

Key points

  • Loam soil is best; sandy soil drains fast and clay holds water.
  • Plough across the slope to stop soil being washed away.
  • N for leaves, P for roots, K for strong plants and fruit.
  • Yellow old leaves can mean nitrogen shortage; report what you see.
  • Apply only the amount of fertiliser you are told, away from stems.
  • Compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly and smells like soil.
